one_liner: AssemblyScript Game Boy/Color emulator whose one core builds to both Wasm and JS; benchmark app compares them per frame.
what_it_does: WasmBoy is a Game Boy / Game Boy Color emulator library (npm package wasmboy, 0.7.1) whose core is written in AssemblyScript and compiled to WebAssembly, with a JS lib layer that drives it from Web Workers in the browser or Node (headless option). The same core source can also be compiled by the TypeScript compiler to plain JavaScript, with Wasm memory replaced by a typed array, and the repo's demo/benchmark app runs the Wasm core, that JS core and a Closure-compiled JS core on the same ROM and config to compare frame times. For the catalogue it is mainly a like-for-like AssemblyScript-Wasm versus JavaScript case study, not a drop-in replacement for any JS library.
how_it_is_fast: The core is written as statically typed AssemblyScript (i32/u8 integer arithmetic on a flat linear memory, with the Game Boy memory map, VRAM, frame buffer and audio buffers at fixed offsets) and compiled by asc with -O3 --converge, so the Wasm build runs integer-only code with no deoptimisation risk. The JS build of the same source keeps the arithmetic but relies on explicit *Portable helpers (param & 0xff, | 0) to mimic Wasm integer wrap-around, and every load/store goes through a JS function indexing a Uint8ClampedArray, so engine type speculation and bounds checks are what Wasm saves. Lib-level speedups (audio batch processing, accumulated samples, tile caching) are config options applied equally to all cores in the benchmark.
when_to_use: Embedding a Game Boy / Game Boy Color emulator in a web page or Node tool where GPL-3.0-or-later is acceptable, for homebrew or playable commercial ROMs that do not need cycle accuracy.

As a reference case of a large real-world AssemblyScript codebase compiled to both Wasm and JS from one source, to study Wasm-versus-JS frame-time differences per browser with the demo/benchmark runner.
Teaching or debugging GB internals: the debugger demo exposes per-cycle CPU, PPU, APU, timer and memory state, breakpoints and tile and background map views.

Low-end devices where the documented performance options (audioBatchProcessing, audioAccumulateSamples, tileCaching) are acceptable; the repo's own Node table shows audio batch processing cutting 1,250 frames from 3,338 ms to 2,032 ms on back-to-color.gbc.
when_not_to_use: Accuracy-critical emulation: the README says 'the emulator is still not very accurate. Expect bugs' and the project never reached 1.0; serial interrupts are not implemented, so many mooneye tests fail.
Closed-source or permissive-licence products: the core and lib are GPL-3.0-or-later.

Projects that need a maintained toolchain: last code release 0.7.1 on 2022-03-25, only dependabot bumps afterwards (last 2022-10-12), pinned to assemblyscript ^0.15.1 and typescript ^3.1.3, and one runtime dependency is a git URL to the author's fork of audiobuffer-to-wav.

Expecting a published Wasm-versus-JS speedup figure: the repo commits no benchmark numbers, the first-party Medium article is unreachable here, and the gain is browser-dependent (the 2022 De Macedo et al. study reports Firefox favouring JavaScript; issue #308 reports the JS cores at about half Chrome's FPS in Firefox).

Using the JS (TypeScript-compiled) core as a product: the maintainer said it 'wasn't meant to be playable as a user', and its memory mock is byte-granular, so save-state load<i32>/store<i32> calls read and write a single clamped byte.

integration.form: npm module (wasmboy; ESM, CJS, UMD and IIFE bundles with the Wasm core inlined) or build the AssemblyScript core yourself
integration.dependencies: idb, raf, responsive-gamepad 1.1.0, audiobuffer-to-wav (git URL to torch2424's es-module-rollup branch); build needs assemblyscript ^0.15.1, typescript ^3.1.3, rollup and Closure Compiler plugins
integration.min_toolchain: AssemblyScript 0.15.x for the core (newer versions not tested by the project); browsers with WebAssembly and Web Workers; Node needs worker_threads (--experimental-worker on old Node)
integration.platforms: Chrome, Firefox and Safari targeted; Node via the headless option
integration.thread_safety: Lib runs the core in Web Workers; a core instance is single-threaded with module-level global state (one emulator per instance)

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the first-party numbers: the Medium article (linked from issue #214, opened 2018-12-20) predates fix PR #218 (commit 838af61, 2018-12-22). Before it, the JS core indexed its typed array with non-integer offsets such as 59853.5 from a division in channel3.ts (issue #216), because Wasm's integer division became a float division in JS. The JS baseline therefore read undefined audio samples, so it did different work from the Wasm core, and it triggered a SpiderMonkey recompilation loop (Bugzilla 1515620). The maintainer also said he had forgotten to recompile the Closure build that night ('it was definitely my fault'), so the article's JS and Closure columns, Firefox's especially, were measured on a buggy or stale baseline.

The JS core's memory mock is a Uint8ClampedArray: stores saturate where Wasm's store8 wraps, and load/store ignore the type parameter. JS-versus-Wasm equivalence rests on hand-placed i32Portable/u8Portable calls (114 in cpu/opcodes.ts), and the benchmark never checks that the cores produce identical frames or audio.

demo/benchmark times each executeFrame() with the microseconds package, which in a browser uses performance.now(). Browsers coarsen that clock (Spectre mitigations), and one emulated frame takes only about 1.4-2.7 ms (the repo's Node table: 1,250 frames in 1,690-3,338 ms), so the min, max and mode rows are quantised; only the mean is usable. Cores run one after another rather than interleaved, the first 15% of each run is dropped, and canvas rendering plus a growing times array copied every frame (garbage-collector pressure) sit between timed frames.

The benchmark applies one config to all cores (audioBatchProcessing, audioAccumulateSamples and tileCaching on, boot ROM off), so its results are not default-config emulator speed. test/performance/results.md shows these options alone change frame time by up to 1.7x.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick WasmBoy over tinymt-wasm-typescript-benchmark, Speedy.js or rsmod-pathfinder when you want a whole application (CPU, PPU, APU, timers) compiled from one AssemblyScript source to both Wasm and JS, rather than a single kernel. Pick rsmod-pathfinder or tinymt when you need committed, reproducible numbers, which WasmBoy does not ship.
verified_claims_summary: No numbers are committed. The repo's runner times the AssemblyScript Wasm core (asc -O3 --converge) against the same source compiled by tsc to JS, and the same JS run through Closure, per emulated frame in the browser (default 2,500 frames, mean of the last 85%). The only figures seen are search snippets of De Macedo et al. 2022: six games in Chrome, Edge and Firefox, Wasm faster overall but Firefox favouring JavaScript, with no CPU or version stated. The first-party Medium article was out by 2018-12-20 (issue #214 asks to link it), so it measured a JS core that still had the non-integer-index bug fixed in PR #218 two days later, unless it was revised afterwards (the maintainer promised an update in issue #216; the article could not be opened here).
status_note: Abandoned: last code release 0.7.1 (2022-03-25), only dependabot merges to 2022-10-12, 76 open issues. GPL-3.0-or-later, so copyable only into GPL-compatible projects, and the evidence is snippet-only and browser-dependent; the first-party article's JS baseline predates a correctness fix (issue #216, PR #218).
